summary: Describes the UTF-16 encoding of Unicode and ISO 10646, how to serialize it as bytes for transmission, and the MIME charset naming and registration. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Computers turn letters into numbers. UTF-16 is one way to do it, including for symbols from many languages.

questions: how is utf-16 sent over the internet
what is a byte order mark
subtitle: A 16-bit encoding for the world's writing systems.

tldr.problem: Programs need a way to represent all the world's characters (from Unicode and ISO 10646) as bytes for storage and transmission, with efficiency and a defined byte order.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-16 encodes characters as either one or two 16-bit values. Characters below 0x10000 are single values; characters from 0x10000 to 0x10FFFF are pairs of surrogates. The byte order (big-endian or little-endian) is specified via a label or byte-order mark.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2781 is still the standard definition of UTF-16 and defines three MIME charset labels. Though UTF-8 is more common on the Internet, UTF-16 remains important in systems and formats that adopted it.

today: RFC 2781 remains the standard definition of UTF-16 and is not obsoleted. However, UTF-8 has become far more common in Internet protocols and on the web, while UTF-16 remains important in many application frameworks and formats, particularly in systems that use 16-bit character types.

sections.title: What UTF-16 Is
sections.content:
RFC 2781 defines UTF-16, an encoding of the Unicode and ISO 10646 character sets. It lets any program on the Internet agree on how to turn letters, symbols, and characters from any language into a stream of bytes that can be stored in a file or sent over a network.

UTF-16 is one of three standard ways to encode Unicode; the others are UTF-8 and UTF-32. Unlike UTF-8, which uses variable-length byte sequences, UTF-16 always uses 16-bit units. This makes it useful in systems that are built around 16-bit processing, such as Java.
sections.eli5: UTF-16 is a rule book that says how to turn each letter or symbol from the world's alphabets into 16-bit numbers and then into bytes.

sections.title: How Characters Are Encoded
sections.content:
UTF-16 uses two rules. Characters with values less than 0x10000 (the first 65,536 characters, known as the Basic Multilingual Plane or BMP) are represented as a single 16-bit value equal to the character's number. For example, the letter 'A' is 0x0041.

Characters with values from 0x10000 to 0x10FFFF are encoded as two 16-bit values called surrogates. The encoding algorithm subtracts 0x10000 from the character value, then splits the result into two 10-bit parts. The high part is added to 0xD800 (a high surrogate), and the low part is added to 0xDC00 (a low surrogate). Values between 0xD800 and 0xDFFF are reserved for surrogates and do not represent actual characters.
sections.eli5: For normal letters and symbols (the first 65,000 or so), UTF-16 writes one 16-bit number. For rare symbols from outer space and beyond, it writes two numbers together.

sections.title: Byte Order and the Byte Order Mark
sections.content:
A single 16-bit value can be written to a byte stream in two ways. Big-endian puts the high-order byte first, then the low-order byte. Little-endian does the opposite. Both are common in computer hardware.

Unicode defines a special character, 0xFEFF, the zero-width non-breaking space, which also serves as a byte order mark (BOM). When this character appears at the very beginning of a UTF-16 stream, it signals the byte order: if the bytes are 0xFE 0xFF, the stream is big-endian; if they are 0xFF 0xFE, it is little-endian. At any other position, 0xFEFF is treated as a real character with no special meaning.
sections.eli5: Computers write two-byte numbers in different orders: some put the big byte first, others the little byte first. A special marker at the start can tell you which way it is.

sections.title: MIME Charset Labels
sections.content:
RFC 2781 registers three MIME charset labels for use in email headers and web content types:

  • UTF-16BE: Big-endian UTF-16 without a byte order mark. Applications reading this label know the data is big-endian.
  • UTF-16LE: Little-endian UTF-16 without a byte order mark. Applications reading this label know the data is little-endian.
  • UTF-16: UTF-16 with unknown byte order. The sender should prepend a byte order mark, and the receiver must read the first two bytes to detect the order. If there is no BOM, the default is big-endian.

The RFC clarifies that UTF-16 charsets are not suitable for use in MIME 'text' top-level media types because they do not encode line endings in the MIME-required way, except that HTTP is exempt from this restriction.
sections.eli5: When you send UTF-16 data, you label it to tell the receiver which byte order to expect, or you start with a magic signal so they can figure it out.

sections.title: Security and Considerations
sections.content:
Processors handling UTF-16 text must account for several security issues. Character sets are frequently extended with new characters. Processors must handle unknown characters safely and not allow them to be exploited to harm the recipient. Additionally, text can contain control characters that might reprogram a display or keyboard, or special characters like the Object Replacement Character (0xFFFC) that can trigger external processing with unintended side effects.

Implementors must carefully handle illegal UTF-16 sequences: surrogate pairs with illegal values, unpaired surrogates, or other violations of the UTF-16 syntax. A naive parser could be exploited to behave anomalously when given malformed byte sequences.
sections.eli5: Be careful when you read UTF-16: strange characters or broken encoding can sometimes trick programs or cause them to do things they should not.

viz.caption: UTF-16 encoding for characters in the BMP

fields.name: Character Value
fields.desc: Any value from 0x0000 to 0xFFFF except 0xD800–0xDFFF (surrogate range).

viz.caption: UTF-16 encoding for characters outside the BMP

fields.name: High Surrogate
fields.desc: Value between 0xD800 and 0xDBFF, containing the high 10 bits of the 20-bit offset.

fields.name: Low Surrogate
fields.desc: Value between 0xDC00 and 0xDFFF, containing the low 10 bits of the 20-bit offset.
